```{r, setup, include = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(mosaicData)
```

## Exercises  {#Exercises_Dates}

### Exercise 1 {-}

Convert the following to date or date/time objects.

**a)** September 13, 2010.
```{r}
mdy('September 13, 2010 ')
```
I converted the full date with no abbreviations.

**b)** Sept 13, 2010.
```{r}
mdy('Sept 13, 2010') #mdy('Sep 13 2010')
```
Sept does not work with mdy. Also you have to remove the comma after the day.(Actually, comma does not matter)

**c)** Sep 13, 2010.
```{r}
mdy('Sep 13, 2010') 
```
The abbreviation 'Sep' worked for September - can use comma - R will ignore it 

**d)** S 13, 2010. Comment on the month abbreviation needs.
```{r}
mdy('S 13 2010') #mdy('Sep 13 2010')
```
S is not enough information for the month - need the full abreviation 'Sep'for mdy to run.

**e)** 07-Dec-1941.
```{r}
dmy('07-Dec-1941')
```
The 3 letters for month worked in this case as well. 

**f)** 1-5-1998. Comment on why you might be wrong.
```{r}
mdy('1-5-1998')
dmy('1-5-1998')
```
Don't know whether the correct format for this is month/day/year or day/month/year

**g)** 21-5-1998. Comment on why you know you are correct.
```{r}
dmy('21-5-1998')
```
This is correct because day can be 1-31, but month can only be 1-12. 

**h)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am
```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am')
```

**i)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am PDT (ex Seattle)

```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am', tz='America/Los_Angeles')
```
Can specify time zon with tz

**j)** 2020-May-5 10:30 am AST (ex Puerto Rico)
```{r}
ymd_hm('2020-May-5 10:30 am', tz='America/Puerto_Rico')
```

### Exercise 3 {-}

Suppose you have arranged for a phone call to be at 3 pm on May 8, 2025 at Arizona time. However, the recipient will be in Auckland, NZ. What time will it be there? 

```{r}
mdy_hm('May 8, 2025 3:00 PM', tz = 'US/Arizona') %>% with_tz(tzone = 'Pacific/Auckland') #Use with_tz in order to convert time zones
```
I used with_tz to convert the time from Arizona time to the time in Auckland. 

### Exercise 4 {-}

From this book's [GitHub](https://github.com/BuscagliaR/STA_444_v2/) directory, navigate to the `data-raw` directory and then download the `Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv` data file. (*There are several weather station files. Make sure you get the correct one!*)  There is a `DATE` column (is it of type `date` when you import the data?) as well as the Maximum and Minimum temperature. For the last 5 years of data included in the file, plot the time series of daily maximum temperature with date on the x-axis. Write your code so that it will work if I update the date set. *Hint: Find the maximum date in the data set and then subtract 5 years. Will there be a difference if you use `dyears(5)` vs `years(5)`? Which seems more appropriate here?*

```{r}
Pul_Weather <- read.csv("../data-raw/Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv") 
#Here had to do .. in order for it to retrieve the correct file

Pul_Weather <- Pul_Weather %>%
  mutate(DATE = ymd(DATE)) #Makes the date an actual date so we can maniuplate it 

#Start <- max(Pul_Weather$DATE)
End   <- max(Pul_Weather$DATE) - years(5) #tried to do an interval here which kind of worked? It ended up working nicely though because I saved the desired dates to an object and then plugged that into my filter

#d2  <- max(Pul_Weather$DATE) - dyears(5)

Pul_Weather_5 <- Pul_Weather %>%
  filter(DATE >= End) #Filters columns - Need a logial for filter

ggplot(data= Pul_Weather_5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = DATE, y = TMAX, color = TMAX))+
  labs(x = 'Time (Year)', y = 'Maximum Temp.')


```


### Exercise 5 {-}

It turns out there is some interesting periodicity regarding the number of births on particular days of the year.

**a)** Using the `mosaicData` package, load the data set `Births78` which records the number of children born on each day in the United States in 1978. Because this problem is intended to show how to calculate the information using the `date`, remove all the columns *except* `date` and `births`.

```{r}
#View(Births78)

Births78 <- Births78 %>%
  select(date, births) %>%
  mutate(date = ymd(date)) #Again, making sure sates are in a manipulateable form 
```
I loaded Births78 and used the select function to select the columns date and births, and then mutated the dates to the appropriat format using the lubridate function ymd.

**b)** Graph the number of `births` vs the `date` with date on the x-axis. What stands out to you? Why do you think we have this trend?
```{r}
ggplot(data=Births78) +
  geom_point(aes(x=date, y=births))
```
There was a higher number of births in the summer/early fall of 1978 than the beginning of 1978. There is also a significant separation between number of births that are likely explained by days of the week in which babies are born.


**c)** To test your assumption, we need to figure out the what day of the week each observation is. Use `dplyr::mutate` to add a new column named `dow` that is the day of the week (Monday, Tuesday, etc). This calculation will involve some function in the `lubridate` package and the `date` column.

```{r}
Births78 <- Births78 %>%
  mutate('dow' = wday(date, label = TRUE)) #Adds a new column - day of the week - Gives us a way to differentiate data into days of the week - We are going to end up recoloring points according to day of the week 
```
I added a new column using the mutate function and then the lubridate command wday() to extract the abbreviation for day of the week. 

**d)** Plot the data with the point color being determined by the day of the week variable.

```{r}
ggplot(data=Births78) +
  geom_point(aes(x=date, y=births, color = dow))
```
I made a scatter plot similar to the one in part b but colored the points by day of the week in an aesthetics command.
